Volkswagen Negotiations With IG Metall To Begin November 24, Audi Factory In US Rumored

EV
By Dr. Ethan Vance Chief EV & Battery Systems Fellow • via CleanTechnica Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: CleanTechnica Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • Volkswagen Group is desperate to cut costs.
  • As recently as 2023, the company had an operating profit of €22.6 billion, but by 2025, that number had been slashed to €8.9 billion.
  • 2026 may be half of that.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • DR. ETHAN VANCE Chief EV & Battery Systems Fellow

The Electrification & Charging Infrastructure Horizon

Beyond the immediate headline, this development marks a critical inflection point in the broader EV transition. As automakers and charging networks race to lower consumer friction, the reporting from CleanTechnica highlights that battery energy density, thermal management, and raw cost per kilowatt-hour remain the ultimate battlegrounds. For prospective EV buyers and fleet operators, tracking these operational metrics offers clear guidance on vehicle longevity and residual value.

Big Picture: Global battery production scale and grid upgrades will define whether mass-market adoption targets are met over the next 24 months.

Volkswagen Group is desperate to cut costs. As recently as 2023, the company had an operating profit of €22.6 billion, but by 2025, that number had been slashed to €8.9 billion. 2026 may be half of that. In today’s market, it has more factory capacity in Germany that it needs, which has led to a proposal to shutter as many as four of them and reduce its domestic workforce by 50,000 workers. Globally, it plans to eliminate up to 100,000 jobs over the next four years. It expects its austerity plans to create €20 ⁠billion in savings across its entire value chain by 2030, while lowering ​overhead costs by €11 billion. Reportedly, it plans to stop making half of its existing models .

📌 The Core Development

On September 30, 2026, Volkswagen Group announced it was terminating many of the wage provisions it agreed to in December, 2024 with IG Metall, the union that represents many of Volkswagen’s workers. According to Reuters , the terminated provisions included wage agreements that cover more than 100,000 workers at Volkswagen’s primary factories in Germany. Those agreements govern such things as working hours and holiday pay, provisions that IG Metal sees as benefits it won for workers after long and often contentious negotiations with the company.

The last time Volkswagen cancelled parts of its collective bargaining framework with the ​union was in September, 2024. That triggered ​a wave of strikes ⁠that culminated in a landmark labor deal in December, 2024 that included 35,000 job cuts. Part of that agreement provided either side could revisit the terms of the agreement if there was a material change in circumstances.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The company says its deteriorating finances justify its decision to cancel the wage provisions previously agreed to. Human resources chief Arne Meiswinkel said management was acting to ensure the company ​remains fit for the future. “We must continue to work on our cost structures,” he said. Terminating the agreements “gives us room to negotiate ‌so that ⁠we can then agree on the necessary measures.”

Despite that justification by the company, the union and the workers are furious. IG Metall representative Thorsten Groeger thundered, “This is a despicable blow to the workforce. We will not accept this. Anyone who tries to reach into the employees’ pockets must ​expect a fight.”

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

IG Metall is contractually bound not to strike the company until January 1, 2027, but it is rattling its sabers and warning that strikes will be starting as soon as that deadline passes if the company’s plan not to honor the 2024 agreement is not rescinded by October 31. “We are giving the company until the end of October to withdraw this notice of ​termination,” Thorsten Groeger said in Hanover, where unions and management met for a fresh round of talks last week. “Otherwise a massive process will be set in motion which, let me make this clear, will pave the way for industrial action at Volkswagen.”

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

“The economic situation has deteriorated dramatically since the collective bargaining agreement for the future was concluded in 2024. This creates an urgent need for action,” Arne Meiswinkel said after ​the two sides met in Hannover last week. After that meeting, the works council said the company’s executive board plans to freeze the salaries of 660,000 staff worldwide until 2030. The union is not amused. “We know which operating conditions have changed, but we also know which ones ​were foreseeable, and we expect the highest-paid management board in this country to work with ​us to find ⁠a solution,” said works council chief Daniela Cavallo.
